## Why this matters

Every LLM launch comes with a scorecard. GPQA up 7%. MMLU-Pro at the top. HumanEval crushed. These numbers travel fast in product meetings and procurement docs. They rarely travel with context.

The problem isn’t that benchmarks exist. It’s how they’re consumed. A cholesterol test doesn’t predict blood pressure. An ECG doesn’t measure lung function. Each test answers a specific question. The diagnosis comes from the pattern, not the headline.

LLM benchmarks follow the same logic. GPQA tests reasoning on hard science questions. MMLU-Pro tests broad knowledge under adversarial formatting. HumanEval tests function-level coding. None of these tells you how the model behaves under load, with real users, in your actual use case. The score is a starting point. Treating it as a verdict is where teams get burned.

## First principles: what a benchmark really measures

A benchmark is a measurement instrument. It tells you how a model performs under a specific task format, metric, and protocol. It does not automatically predict how that model will behave in your production workflow.

Most benchmarks emphasize one or two capability “muscles”: factual recall, multi-step reasoning, code correctness, repository-level engineering, long-context retrieval, or multi-turn dialogue quality. Strong evaluation therefore needs a portfolio, not a single headline number.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/0*yZSZicHNghrxTXfk)

Teams that skip this discipline often drift into benchmark theater: great leaderboard optics, disappointing product outcomes.

## GPQA: why everyone is talking about it

GPQA (Graduate-Level Google-Proof QA) gets attention because it targets hard science questions written by domain experts. It is intentionally difficult for both non-experts and current frontier models, which makes it a high-signal stress test for advanced reasoning.

In practice, GPQA is reported as accuracy under controlled multiple-choice settings. Strategically, teams use it to test whether a model can reason through challenging scientific prompts instead of relying on shallow retrieval patterns.

A useful analogy is an oral exam with a strict PhD committee. Passing that exam suggests depth in a narrow domain. It does not prove the same model can debug real repositories, handle customer chat safely, or execute tool-heavy workflows.

Source: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022)

## MMLU and MMLU-Pro: broad academic checks

MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) became a default benchmark because it covers 57 subjects spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional topics. It gives a broad snapshot of knowledge and basic reasoning, making it useful as a first-pass “general coverage” check.

As models improved, MMLU often became less discriminative near the top — many strong models now score above 85%. MMLU-Pro (Professional) raises difficulty by adding reasoning-heavy questions, more adversarial answer formatting, and domain-specific challenges, making it more useful when comparing frontier models.

Think of MMLU as a broad standardized exam and MMLU-Pro as the honors version. Both are helpful for breadth checks. Neither should be treated as a production readiness certificate.

Sources:

- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300)
- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574)

## GSM8K and MATH: quantitative reasoning under pressure

If your product depends on quantitative reasoning, math benchmarks matter. GSM8K focuses on multi-step grade-school word problems, while MATH pushes into competition-level problem solving.

These benchmarks are valuable because they expose brittle reasoning chains that broad benchmarks can hide. A model may look strong on general QA and still fail on arithmetic consistency, intermediate-step logic, or symbolic reasoning.

A practical analogy: GSM8K is a disciplined “show your work” worksheet; MATH is closer to olympiad-style challenge sets. If you operate in analytics, finance, STEM tutoring, or scientific tooling, include at least one in your core suite.

Sources:

- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168)
- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03874](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03874)

## HumanEval and SWE-bench: coding is not one skill

A common mistake is treating coding performance as one capability. HumanEval and SWE-bench make clear that it is at least two very different skills.

HumanEval measures function-level code generation correctness, typically via executable tests and pass@k metrics. It is clean, reproducible, and good for first-pass coding quality.

SWE-bench is much closer to real engineering work. It asks models to resolve real GitHub issues in real repositories, requiring cross-file reasoning, dependency awareness, and practical debugging judgment.

The analogy is straightforward: HumanEval is a coding interview question; SWE-bench is an on-call fix in a live codebase. Strong performance on both is more meaningful than a win on either one alone.

Sources:

- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374)
- [https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)

## MT-Bench and HELM: conversation quality and holistic reporting

For assistant products, quality is not only factual correctness. It also includes coherence across turns, calibration under uncertainty, and behavioral consistency. MT-Bench became popular for this conversational layer, often combining LLM-as-judge signals with human comparison.

The caveat is bias: judge choice, response length effects, and phrasing artifacts can move scores. HELM-style evaluation frameworks help by forcing broader scenario coverage and multi-metric reporting, reducing over-claim risk from a single chat leaderboard.

Think of this as moving from one lab number to a full clinical panel: more work, but far better diagnosis.

## A practical benchmark portfolio you can actually run

For a general-purpose LLM assistant, start with a compact but diverse portfolio. The goal is not maximum benchmark count. The goal is capability coverage aligned to user-facing risk.

Recommended starter set:

- **Depth reasoning:** GPQA
- **Broad reasoning:** MMLU-Pro
- **Math reasoning:** GSM8K or MATH
- **Coding quality:** HumanEval
- **Real engineering tasks:** SWE-bench
- **Conversation quality:** MT-Bench
- **Reporting discipline:** HELM-style multi-metric output

Then add a layer many teams skip: production correlation. Track whether benchmark movement predicts real KPI movement (task success, deflection rate, CSAT, ticket volume, bug reopen rate). If correlation is weak, rebalance the suite.

## Anti-patterns that create benchmark theater

Benchmark misuse is usually predictable. Make these failure modes explicit in your review checklist:

- **Cherry-picking datasets:** only reporting tasks where the model wins.
- **Single-metric reporting:** publishing accuracy without robustness, calibration, or efficiency context.
- **Protocol mismatch:** comparing scores from different prompts, decoding settings, or tool policies.
- **Ignoring variance:** presenting one run as truth without uncertainty bounds.
- **Skipping contamination checks:** not testing for train/eval overlap risk.
- **No production validation:** assuming leaderboard gains transfer directly to user outcomes.

A simple control helps: every benchmark report should include a mandatory “limitations and caveats” section. If that section is missing, the report is incomplete.

## Leakage and contamination: the silent score inflator

One of the most important technical risks in LLM benchmarking is contamination. If benchmark content appears in pretraining or post-training corpora, scores can look excellent while true generalization remains weak.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/0*Apl9QWyHCjde-NFo)

Minimum safeguards:

- compare benchmark publication date vs model training cutoff,
- run paraphrased variants to test brittle memorization,
- investigate suspiciously high zero-shot behavior on public tasks,
- maintain at least one private or freshly curated eval set for your domain.

Contamination is similar to exam answer-key leakage. The score is numerically real, but its meaning changes. Without leakage audits, benchmark claims are hard to trust.

Source framing: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04615](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04615)

## Reporting template teams can copy

When sharing benchmark results internally or externally, use a fixed reporting template so comparisons stay reproducible and decision-grade.

Include:

- model/version and training cutoff,
- benchmark version and evaluation harness,
- prompt template + decoding settings,
- metric definitions (for example, pass@1 vs pass@10),
- mean/variance or confidence intervals,
- caveats (contamination risk, domain mismatch),
- production proxy metric movement -whether improvements in benchmark scores actually correlate with improvements in real-world performance

This discipline adds small overhead, but prevents expensive model-selection mistakes caused by incomplete scorecards.

## Final takeaway

Benchmarks are essential when treated as instruments, not trophies.

GPQA gives high-value signal for hard scientific reasoning. MMLU-Pro provides broad rigor. GSM8K/MATH test quantitative chains. HumanEval and SWE-bench separate snippet coding from real engineering work. MT-Bench measures conversational behavior. HELM-style reporting keeps interpretation honest.

If you remember one line, use this: evaluate LLMs like a diagnostic panel, not a single test result. That shift alone reduces benchmark theater and improves production model selection.

# LLM Benchmarks Compared: MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K and More (2026)

Nov 06, 2025

Written by [LXT](https://www.lxt.ai/blog/author/lxt/)

![llm benchmarking abstract illustration](https://s40145.pcdn.co/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/llm-benchmarks.webp)

**LLM benchmarks are standardised tests that measure model capability across reasoning, coding, mathematics, language understanding, and agentic task completion.** In 2026, 15 major benchmarks are in active use. Most measure academic performance on fixed tasks, while only four reliably predict real production outcomes. This guide explains what each benchmark measures, shows current scores for six frontier models, and answers the question leaderboard sites don’t: which benchmarks should you actually run for your specific use case.

For live scores updated weekly, [LiveBench](https://livebench.ai/) and [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) are the authoritative references. This guide covers something different: what those scores actually test, where they break down for enterprise production environments, and how to build an evaluation program that goes beyond public benchmarks — including the benchmark gap no leaderboard addresses, locale-level capability.

## Why LLM benchmark scores often don’t transfer to production

Benchmark scores fail to predict production performance for two reasons: saturation and data contamination. A saturated benchmark is one where leading models have already reached near-ceiling scores, so the benchmark no longer distinguishes between good and great. A contaminated benchmark is one where the test questions appeared in the model’s training data, making the score an artifact of memorisation rather than reasoning.

LXT Training Data

Your flywheel is only as fast as your annotation pipeline.

LXT embeds into your retraining loop, delivering labeled data at the cadence your model demands, not months later.

[Talk to our team](https://www.lxt.ai/contact/)

GSM8K, the grade school math benchmark, illustrates both problems. When it launched in 2021, it was challenging: GPT-3 scored around 35%. By 2024, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, and Gemini 1.5 all exceeded 90%. Today, GPT-5.3 Codex scores 99%. The benchmark has saturated completely for frontier model comparisons. More seriously, a 2023 study showed that removing contaminated examples from the GSM8K test set produced accuracy drops of up to 13% for some models, meaning a meaningful portion of high scores were driven by training set overlap rather than genuine mathematical reasoning.

The result is that a model’s published benchmark score predicts production performance only when three conditions hold: the benchmark tests tasks similar to your use case, the test set is clean of training data contamination, and the benchmark hasn’t saturated to the point where score differences are statistically meaningless.

| Benchmark | Top score (Feb 2026) | Saturated? | Why it still matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K | 99% (GPT-5.3 Codex) | Yes | Useful for evaluating smaller or fine-tuned models; meaningless for frontier comparisons |
| MMLU | 93% (GPT-5.3 Codex) | Yes | Broad coverage; still differentiates mid-tier models, not frontier |
| HellaSwag | 95%+ (multiple models) | Yes | Useful baseline check for smaller models and fine-tuned variants |
| GPQA Diamond | 94.3% (Gemini 3.1 Pro) | Approaching | Still differentiates top frontier models; approaching saturation among leaders |
| SWE-bench Verified | 80.8% (Claude Opus 4.6) | No | Real software engineering tasks; contamination-resistant and actively improving |
| HLE | 53.1% with tools (Claude Opus 4.6) | No | Designed to stay unsaturated; the current frontier difficulty benchmark |

## The 15 most-cited LLM benchmarks: what each one tests

Each benchmark targets a distinct capability. Here are the 15 most widely used LLM benchmarks in 2026, organised by category. The master table below is the fastest way to find the benchmark that maps to your evaluation goal.

| Benchmark | Category | What it measures | Top model + score (Feb 2026) | Saturated? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MMLU | Reasoning / knowledge | 57 academic subjects, 16,000+ multiple-choice questions | GPT-5.3 Codex — 93% | Yes |
| BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) | Reasoning | 23 complex reasoning tasks designed to resist shortcuts | Frontier models — 90%+ | Partially |
| HellaSwag | Commonsense reasoning | Sentence completion requiring commonsense inference | Multiple models — 95%+ | Yes |
| GPQA Diamond | Expert reasoning | PhD-level science questions in biology, chemistry, physics | Gemini 3.1 Pro — 94.3% | Approaching |
| HumanEval | Code generation | 164 Python programming tasks with functional correctness testing | GPT-5.3 Codex — 93% | Yes |
| HumanEval+ | Code generation | HumanEval with extended test coverage to reduce false positives | Frontier models — ~85%+ | Partially |
| SWE-bench Verified | Software engineering | Real GitHub issues resolved end-to-end in a live codebase | Claude Opus 4.6 — 80.8% | No |
| LiveCodeBench | Code generation | Contamination-resistant coding evaluation with rolling question updates | Qwen3.5-plus — 83.6% | No |
| GSM8K | Math reasoning | Grade school math, 8,500 word problems | GPT-5.3 Codex — 99% | Yes |
| MATH-500 | Math reasoning | 500 competition-level math problems across 5 difficulty levels | GPT-5.3 Codex — 96% | Partially |
| MGSM | Multilingual math | GSM8K problems translated into 10 languages | GPT-5.3 Codex — 96% | Partially |
| TruthfulQA | Safety / factuality | 817 questions designed to elicit hallucinations from models that mimic common misconceptions | Frontier models — 85%+ | Partially |
| HELM | Holistic evaluation | Multi-metric evaluation across accuracy, calibration, fairness, and efficiency | Composite — varies by dimension | No |
| GAIA | Agentic tasks | Real-world tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, tool use, and information retrieval | Agent-dependent — top systems 85%+ (L1) | No |
| HLE | Frontier / contamination-resistant | 2,500 expert-level questions from domain specialists; designed to stay difficult as models improve | Claude Opus 4.6 — 53.1% (with tools) | No |

### Reasoning and knowledge: MMLU, BIG-Bench Hard, HellaSwag, GPQA-Diamond

**MMLU measures reasoning and knowledge across 57 academic subjects**, from elementary mathematics to professional law and medicine. Its 16,000+ multiple-choice questions make it the most widely cited general-capability benchmark. The limitation: frontier models have saturated it above 88%, and GPT-5.3 Codex now scores 93%. MMLU scores no longer differentiate between leading models. It remains useful for evaluating smaller and mid-tier models where the spread is still informative.

**BIG-Bench Hard tests complex multi-step reasoning across 23 tasks** specifically designed to resist shortcut solutions. Tasks include logical deduction, causal reasoning, and algorithmic problems. Unlike MMLU, BBH requires chain-of-thought reasoning to score well, which makes it more predictive of real-world reasoning performance for models below the frontier tier.

**HellaSwag measures commonsense reasoning through sentence completion**. Given a scenario description, the model must select the most plausible continuation from four options. Like MMLU, HellaSwag has saturated for frontier models at 95%+. It remains useful as a baseline check for smaller models and fine-tuned variants.

**GPQA-Diamond tests expert-level reasoning on PhD-level science questions** in biology, chemistry, and physics. Questions are designed so that non-expert PhD holders score around 34%, providing a meaningful floor. As of February 2026, Gemini 3.1 Pro leads at 94.3%, Claude Opus 4.6 at 91.3%, and GPT-5.3 Codex at 81%, with Qwen3.5-plus close behind at 88.4%. The benchmark is approaching saturation at the very top of the frontier but still clearly differentiates models in the 60-90% range.

### Code and software engineering: HumanEval, HumanEval+, SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench

**HumanEval measures code generation quality across 164 Python programming tasks**, testing each completion with unit tests to check functional correctness. It is the standard coding benchmark cited in model release papers. The limitation: frontier models including GPT-5.3 Codex now score 93%, and training set contamination is well-documented. For current frontier model comparisons, LiveCodeBench or SWE-bench Verified are more reliable.

**HumanEval+ extends HumanEval with an expanded test suite** that catches more edge cases and reduces false positives. A model that passes the basic HumanEval test may fail HumanEval+ on the same task because the additional tests expose incomplete implementations. Score gaps between HumanEval and HumanEval+ reveal code quality issues invisible to the original benchmark.

**SWE-bench Verified measures a model’s ability to resolve real GitHub issues** in open-source codebases. Unlike HumanEval, SWE-bench tasks require understanding an existing codebase, identifying the root cause of a bug, and writing a solution that passes the repository’s test suite. Claude Opus 4.6 leads at 80.8%, MiniMax-M2.5 at 80.2%, and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 80.6%, with GLM-5 and Qwen3.5-plus clustered in the 76-78% range. SWE-bench Verified is highly resistant to contamination because the problems come from real-world software development work.

**LiveCodeBench uses rolling updates to stay contamination-resistant**. New programming questions are added monthly from competitive programming platforms, so models cannot be trained on the test set. Qwen3.5-plus leads at 83.6% on LiveCodeBench v6 as of February 2026. LiveCodeBench is the best choice for tracking coding capability over time as models are updated, because score increases must reflect genuine improvement rather than memorisation.

### Math and logic: GSM8K, MATH-500, MGSM

**GSM8K tests mathematical reasoning across 8,500 grade school word problems**. It was the standard math benchmark from 2021 through 2023. Frontier models now reach 99% (GPT-5.3 Codex), making GSM8K useless for top-tier comparisons. It is still informative for evaluating smaller models and quantifying the gap between fine-tuned and base variants.

**MATH-500 tests competition-level mathematical reasoning** across 500 problems drawn from AMC, AIME, and similar competitions, spanning five difficulty levels. Unlike GSM8K, MATH-500 problems require multi-step symbolic reasoning. GPT-5.3 Codex scores 96%. For harder math evaluation, AIME 2025 and AIME 2026 are now the standard frontier benchmarks, with Qwen3.5-plus scoring 91.3% on AIME 2026 and GPT-5.3 Codex at 94% on AIME 2025.

**MGSM tests mathematical reasoning across 10 languages**, using the same 250 grade school math problems translated into Bengali, Chinese, French, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Telugu, and Thai. For any application that serves non-English users, MGSM reveals whether a model reasons consistently across languages or shows significant capability gaps in lower-resource languages. GPT-5.3 Codex scores 96% on MGSM.

One limitation no benchmark addresses: locale variants. MGSM tests Portuguese, but Brazilian and European Portuguese diverge on vocabulary (“ônibus” vs. “autocarro” for bus), formality registers (Brazilian Portuguese defaults to informal second-person “você” where European Portuguese uses formal constructions), and cultural references that affect how a model interprets and generates natural responses. A model that passes MGSM for Spanish does not guarantee consistent performance across Mexican, Argentine, and Castilian Spanish, which differ in vocabulary, idiom, and formality norms. Canadian and European French split on register and technical vocabulary. Simplified and Traditional Chinese share a script but diverge in vocabulary and usage patterns that reflect decades of linguistic separation.

A model that passes MGSM may still fail any of these locale splits in production. No public benchmark covers this gap. Addressing locale-level capability requires evaluation by native-speaker annotators who understand the specific variant your users speak, not aggregate language scores. For enterprise applications serving users across multiple locales — customer support in Latin America alongside Spain, or healthcare AI across Canadian and French markets — benchmark scores for a language code are not sufficient signal.

### Safety and factuality: TruthfulQA, HELM

**TruthfulQA measures a model’s tendency to produce confident hallucinations** across 817 questions in 38 categories including health, law, finance, and conspiracy theories. Questions are designed to elicit incorrect but plausible-sounding answers that mimic common human misconceptions. A model that scores 30% on TruthfulQA generates false but confident answers nearly 70% of the time when asked about topics where misinformation is common.

**HELM evaluates models holistically across multiple metrics** including accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency. Rather than optimising for a single score, HELM produces a multi-dimensional profile. This makes HELM the appropriate choice for compliance-sensitive applications where accuracy alone is insufficient and safety or fairness properties must also be measured.

### Agentic tasks: GAIA and AgentBench

**GAIA evaluates AI agents on real-world tasks requiring tool use, multi-step reasoning, and information retrieval**. Tasks range from answering factual questions using web search to completing multi-step data analysis. GAIA scores are heavily dependent on the agent framework used, so comparing raw GAIA scores across models without controlling for the prompting setup is not meaningful. Top agent systems built on frontier models now score above 85% on Level 1 tasks.

**AgentBench tests agent performance across diverse interactive environments** including operating systems, databases, knowledge graphs, and web browsers. Unlike static question-answering benchmarks, AgentBench requires sustained goal-directed behaviour over multiple steps. It covers tool use, memory, and planning simultaneously, making it the most comprehensive multi-environment agent benchmark available.

### Frontier difficulty: HLE

**Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) consists of 2,500 expert-level questions** contributed by domain specialists in mathematics, science, law, and other fields. Questions were designed to be beyond the reach of AI systems in 2024. In February 2026, Claude Opus 4.6 leads at 53.1% with tool access, followed by GPT-5.3 Codex at 36% and GLM-5 at 32%. The gap between tool-assisted and non-tool scores is significant, confirming that HLE measures agentic reasoning alongside raw knowledge. HLE is the current frontier benchmark: as models improve, their HLE score will track genuine capability gains on genuinely difficult problems.

## Which LLM benchmark should you use? A use case selection guide

The right benchmark depends on your production task. The matrix below maps common enterprise use cases to the benchmarks most likely to predict performance in your specific context, with notes on what each benchmark misses.

| Use case | Benchmarks to run | Why | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Customer support / dialogue | MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, TruthfulQA | MT-Bench tests multi-turn conversation quality; Chatbot Arena captures preference data from real users; TruthfulQA tests factual accuracy in the categories most likely to produce harmful misinformation | Chatbot Arena scores reflect the preferences of the Arena user pool, which skews toward technical English speakers; results may not reflect your target audience |
| Code generation | LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval+ | LiveCodeBench is contamination-resistant; SWE-bench tests real engineering tasks end-to-end; HumanEval+ catches edge cases basic HumanEval misses | Avoid using original HumanEval as the sole metric for frontier models; at 93% for GPT-5.3 Codex, it no longer differentiates |
| Multilingual / locale-level | MGSM, HELM | MGSM tests mathematical reasoning across 10 languages; HELM includes multi-lingual fairness metrics across tasks | Neither benchmark covers locale variants. MGSM tests Portuguese but not Brazilian vs. European Portuguese, which differ in vocabulary, formality, and cultural context. Supplement with human evaluation by native-speaker annotators for locale-critical applications. |
| RAG / information retrieval | RAGAS, HELM, GAIA | RAGAS tests retrieval quality, grounding, and answer faithfulness; HELM evaluates calibration (critical when models answer from retrieved context); GAIA tests multi-step retrieval and synthesis | RAGAS requires your own document corpus to run meaningfully — generic RAG benchmarks do not reflect your specific data distribution |
| Agentic AI (tool use, multi-step) | GAIA, Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified | GAIA tests multi-step real-world task completion with tools; Terminal-Bench tests agentic coding in live environments; SWE-bench tests code agents on real engineering tasks | Agent benchmarks are evolving fast in 2026. Claude Opus 4.6 leads Terminal-Bench at 65.4%; Gemini 3.1 Pro leads at 68.5%. Check for updates quarterly. |
| Compliance-sensitive (healthcare, legal, finance) | TruthfulQA, HELM, GPQA-Diamond | TruthfulQA specifically tests hallucination in health and law categories; HELM measures fairness and bias alongside accuracy; GPQA-Diamond tests expert-level reasoning in medical and scientific domains | No benchmark covers domain-specific regulatory requirements. Passing HELM does not demonstrate HIPAA compliance or legal professional standards. Human review by domain experts is required in addition to benchmark evaluation. |

## LLM benchmark scores in 2026: six frontier models compared

Here are current scores across seven benchmarks for six widely deployed frontier models as of February 2026. These benchmarks were chosen because they still meaningfully differentiate frontier models — MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K are omitted from this table because all frontier models have saturated them above 90%.

| Claude Opus 4.6 | 91.1% ² | — | 91.3% | 80.8% | 53.1% ³ | — | 65.4% |

## The benchmark-to-production gap: saturation, contamination, and what actually predicts success

A model’s benchmark score predicts production performance only when the benchmark tests tasks similar to your use case and the training data hasn’t contaminated the test set. Both conditions fail more often than benchmark papers acknowledge.

**Saturation means differentiation collapses at the top**. When GPT-5.3, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 all score 88-93% on MMLU, the practical difference between them on a real-world knowledge task cannot be read from the benchmark. The score range has compressed to the point where noise exceeds signal. For saturated benchmarks, the model selection decision must be made on other criteria: latency, cost, instruction-following quality, or domain-specific fine-tuning.

**Contamination means some scores reflect memory, not capability**. The 13% GSM8K accuracy drop observed when contaminated examples were removed is a documented lower bound, not an upper bound. The true effect is larger and harder to measure because most training datasets are not fully disclosed. When a model achieves an unusually high score on an older benchmark, contamination should be the first hypothesis, not the last. GSM8K at 99% is not evidence that GPT-5.3 can solve all grade school math problems — it is evidence that the benchmark has exhausted its usefulness as a differentiator.

**In evaluation programs built for enterprise clients, the most reliable predictor of production success is not a single benchmark score**. The pattern that appears consistently across annotation quality evaluations is this: models that perform well on tasks requiring entity-level precision, where the right answer must name a specific entity, date, product, or person rather than a general category, outperform models with higher overall benchmark scores on real-world tasks where specificity matters. GPQA-Diamond and SWE-bench Verified, both requiring precise, verifiable outputs, show stronger correlation with production performance on enterprise tasks than MMLU or HellaSwag.

**A model’s benchmark score is downstream of its training data quality.** Models that lead on GPQA Diamond have been trained on expert-level content annotated with entity-level precision: not just “this answer is correct” but annotations that identify the specific mechanism, named entity, or causal chain the answer depends on. Generic crowdsourced annotation tells a model what to output. Expert annotation teaches the reasoning chain behind why an output is correct. The difference appears directly in benchmark scores that require multi-step precision reasoning.

This has a direct implication for fine-tuning programs. If your fine-tuned model is not improving on precision-sensitive benchmarks despite more training examples, the bottleneck is annotation quality, not data volume or model architecture. A model fine-tuned on 10,000 ambiguously labelled examples will plateau; the same model fine-tuned on 1,000 carefully annotated examples from domain-expert annotators typically does not. The benchmark ceiling for a fine-tuned model is set by the specificity of its training annotations — which is why teams that invest in annotation quality before scaling data volume consistently outperform teams that do the reverse.

## How to build a benchmark baseline for your LLM evaluation program

A production evaluation baseline requires five components: task mapping, public benchmark selection, a proprietary test set, human-in-the-loop spot checks, and versioning. Here is how to build each one.

1. **Map your use case to measurable task types.** Before selecting any benchmark, define the specific tasks your model will perform in production. A customer support model handles multi-turn dialogue, entity extraction (order numbers, product names), and policy-constrained refusals. A code assistant handles generation, explanation, and debugging across specific languages. A financial analysis model handles numerical reasoning, table interpretation, and document summarisation. Each task type maps to a distinct set of benchmarks. Running MMLU for a code assistant tells you almost nothing useful.
2. **Select 2-3 public benchmarks as proxy signals.** Use the use case matrix above to pick benchmarks that test tasks structurally similar to your production workload. For a code assistant: LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified, HumanEval+. For a multilingual support agent: MGSM plus a human evaluation component. For an agentic research tool: GAIA plus Terminal-Bench 2.0. Limit to 2-3 benchmarks to avoid benchmark overfitting, where model selection optimises for benchmark scores rather than production quality.
3. **Build a proprietary test set of 100-500 examples from your production data.** This is the step most teams skip and most consistently regret. A proprietary test set drawn from real production inputs, labelled by qualified annotators, tests the exact distribution of tasks your model will face. It is immune to contamination by definition and directly measures what you care about. 100 examples is the minimum for statistical reliability; 500 gives you enough examples to segment by task type and find targeted weaknesses. The test set should be rotated every 6 months to prevent the team from implicitly overfitting to it.

4. **Run human spot evaluation on 10% of model outputs.** LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, where you use a second model to score the first model’s outputs, is faster and cheaper than human evaluation but systematically underestimates errors in edge cases. Human evaluators catch failure modes that automated metrics miss: factual errors that are superficially plausible, outputs that are technically accurate but inappropriate for the context, and reasoning chains that reach correct conclusions through flawed logic. A 10% human spot evaluation rate gives you a calibration layer without requiring full human review of every output.
5. **Version, rotate, and track benchmark scores over model iterations.** Benchmark scores are only meaningful as a time series. A score of 82% on your proprietary test set tells you nothing in isolation; 82% after fine-tuning, up from 74% on the same test set before fine-tuning, tells you the fine-tuning improved performance by 8 points on your specific tasks. Version your test sets, record scores for every model update, and rotate the test set periodically to prevent implicit overfitting. Treat your evaluation baseline as a product that requires maintenance, not a one-time measurement.

For organisations building production LLM systems, this five-step baseline is the minimum necessary to make model selection decisions with confidence. Relying on published benchmark scores alone means trusting that the public test set distribution matches your production workload, that contamination hasn’t inflated the scores you are comparing, and that the benchmark hasn’t saturated to the point where score differences are noise. For most enterprise applications, none of those assumptions holds.

After coming across Elon Musk’s tweets (now X posts) on Grok, going through a new research paper, or going through an article on LLM comparisons, have you ever wondered what those weird charts with weird names are? What do they represent, or what do they mean?

Well, fear not; this article will give a good enough overview of the different benchmarks used in academics and industry and why they are so broadly used.

## First, why benchmarks?

To test and measure the performance of several large language models, researchers develop benchmarks to provide a **standardized way** to measure and compare different AI models. Every benchmark here specializes in a particular domain, be it either with reasoning questions, code generation, grade school knowledge or some specific subject knowledge. Having a diverse set of benchmarks helps identify areas where models tend to excel and where they need improvement. These benchmarks therefore help LLMs to outperform their capabilities by having improvements in subsequent generations. These benchmarks also vary highly within tasks and domains, making them robust and general-purpose models and not narrow ones.

Lastly, they aid in monitoring the evolution of AI research over time by demonstrating how models advance with new methods and bigger datasets.

> NOTE: I will keep adding newer datasets to this list with time. Feel free to reply to this post if a newer dataset that isn’t here is popularly used as a benchmark.

**Leaderboards** play a pivotal role in tracking the progress of LLMs’ performance on these benchmarks. They track progress over time, comparing multiple LLMs, fostering competition, and helping guide model selection to future customers of these products.

# Hunyuan Hy3 : Tencent’s 295B Open-Source AI Model Takes on GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, and DeepSeek V4

## How to use Hunyuan Hy3 for free?

[![Mehul Gupta](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*vyvhK_h4zA05mg_Y-n2qBA.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@mehulgupta_7991?source=post_page---byline--8ec6cc26a02c---------------------------------------)

Share

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*SSpc0S4Ed1RCLmEb)

Photo by [H&CO](https://unsplash.com/@hngstrm?utm_source=medium&utm_medium=referral) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/?utm_source=medium&utm_medium=referral)

For years, there was a clear gap between proprietary AI models from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and the open-source ecosystem. Open models were cheaper and customizable, but they often struggled with coding, reasoning, long conversations, and complex agent workflows.

That gap is shrinking rapidly.

> Tencent’s latest **Hy3** is another example of how quickly open-source AI is evolving. While its predecessor, Hy3 Preview, showed promise, the final Hy3 release brings major improvements in reasoning, coding, tool use, long-context understanding, and production reliability.

More importantly, Tencent isn’t positioning Hy3 as just another benchmark champion.

The company claims Hy3 was built to solve real production problems , making AI agents more reliable, reducing hallucinations, improving tool calling, and handling long multi-turn conversations without losing context.

Let’s look at what makes Hy3 interesting.

## What is Hy3?

> Hy3 is Tencent’s latest **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** large language model.

Instead of activating all 295 billion parameters for every request, it intelligently activates only **21 billion parameters**, allowing it to deliver flagship-level performance while keeping inference costs significantly lower.

This design has become increasingly popular because it offers an excellent balance between performance and efficiency.

Some notable examples include:

- DeepSeek
- Mixtral
- Qwen MoE
- DBRX

Hy3 joins this family with one of the largest expert architectures released publicly.

## Hy3 at a Glance

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*HTvGo3EA901Ntk1_P0I5XA.png)

The model supports an impressive **256K token context window**, making it suitable for processing large codebases, lengthy reports, books, research papers, or enterprise documentation.

## Mixture-of-Experts Makes Hy3 Surprisingly Efficient

A common misconception is that a 295B model is extremely expensive to run. That’s not how MoE models work.

> Although Hy3 contains **295 billion parameters**, only **21 billion parameters are activated during inference**.

> Imagine having a company with 192 specialists.
>
> Instead of asking all 192 experts to solve every problem, you only consult the eight most relevant experts for each task.

That’s exactly how Hy3 works. This approach dramatically reduces computation while maintaining high-quality outputs.

## Tencent Focused on Post-Training Instead of Scaling Parameters

Interestingly, Tencent didn’t simply build a larger model. Instead, much of Hy3’s improvement comes from better post-training.

According to Tencent, the team:

- Expanded high-quality supervised training datasets
- Increased reinforcement learning (RL) training
- Improved reasoning datasets
- Added more diverse agent workflows
- Optimized long-context instruction following
- Refined tool-use behavior

This is becoming a major trend across modern LLM development.

Instead of endlessly increasing parameter count, companies are improving data quality and reinforcement learning to extract more capability from existing architectures.

## Benchmark Results: Hy3 Competes with Much Larger Models

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*nVcODGx4h14lmxtD.png)

The benchmark results are impressive.

From the released evaluation charts, Hy3 consistently performs near, or sometimes above, models with two to five times more active compute.

### Agentic Coding

Hy3 performs particularly well on software engineering benchmarks. The released results show improvements across:

- SWE-Bench Multilingual
- SWE-Bench Verified
- SWE-Bench Pro
- Terminal Bench
- NL2Repo

Compared to Hy3 Preview, coding performance improved significantly across every benchmark. One notable example is **SWE-Bench Pro**, where Hy3 improved from **46.0** to **57.9**, representing one of the largest jumps in the release.

Terminal Bench performance also increased from **58.0** to **71.7**, indicating stronger autonomous terminal usage.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*ECgu5VWC64c7U4WB.png)

## Agentic Search

AI agents increasingly need to search documentation, browse websites, and retrieve information. Hy3 also shows substantial improvements here.

> On **BrowseComp**, Hy3 reached **84.2**, putting it very close to leading proprietary models.
>
> DeepSearchQA also improved from **82.8** to **91.0**.

These benchmarks suggest Hy3 is becoming much stronger for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and autonomous browsing workflows.

## Working Agent Performance

Productivity tasks have become one of the most important evaluation categories. Hy3 shows strong gains in:

- Office productivity
- Tool use
- Financial modeling
- Frontend development
- Coding assistants
- Game development

Tencent reports particularly large improvements on:

- MCP Atlas
- Toolathon
- SkillsBench
- ClawEval
- Internal production benchmarks

This makes Hy3 more attractive for enterprise AI agents rather than only chatbot applications.

## STEM and Reasoning

Hy3 also improves across mathematical reasoning and scientific benchmarks. Compared to the preview version, the model performs noticeably better on:

- GPQA Diamond
- USAMO
- MathArena Apex
- FrontierScience
- ArxivMath
- PHYBench

Although GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus still lead some difficult reasoning benchmarks, Hy3 narrows the gap considerably despite activating only 21B parameters.

## Benchmarks Don’t Tell the Whole Story

Tencent makes an interesting point. Public benchmarks often fail to capture how useful a model actually is during daily work.

> Instead of relying only on benchmark leaderboards, Tencent conducted a blind evaluation involving **270 domain experts** using real workplace tasks.

> Hy3 scored **2.67 out of 4**, outperforming GLM-5.1’s **2.51 out of 4**.

The biggest improvements appeared in:

- Frontend engineering
- Data infrastructure
- CI/CD pipelines
- Production software development

This kind of evaluation arguably reflects practical usefulness better than isolated benchmark scores.

## Hy3 Focuses on Production Reliability

One of the most interesting parts of the release isn’t the benchmark table. It’s the engineering improvements. Tencent says the team focused heavily on making Hy3 behave predictably inside production systems.

### Better Tool Calling

Many LLMs struggle with:

- Invalid JSON
- Broken tool arguments
- Failed API calls
- Inconsistent formatting

Tencent reports Hy3 now delivers production-grade reliability across different tool-calling frameworks while improving recovery when tool execution fails.

The company also notes that Hy3 maintains stable performance across different agent scaffolds, with only a small variation in SWE-Bench Verified scores.

For developers building AI agents, this consistency is often more valuable than a slight increase in benchmark scores.

## Lower Hallucination Rates

Hallucinations remain one of the biggest challenges for LLMs. Tencent trained Hy3 with a clear principle:

> Answer when grounded. Admit uncertainty when evidence is missing. Never fabricate information.

According to Tencent’s internal evaluations:

- Hallucination rate dropped from **12.5%** to **5.4%**
- Commonsense errors fell from **25.4%** to **12.7%**

While these are internal measurements rather than standardized public benchmarks, they indicate a strong emphasis on factual reliability.

## Stronger Multi-Turn Conversations

Many AI assistants perform well in a single prompt but gradually lose track of user intent during longer conversations. Tencent specifically optimized Hy3 for:

- Coreference resolution
- Multi-turn instruction following
- Context inheritance
- Long conversation consistency
- Ellipsis recovery

> Internal testing reduced multi-turn conversation issues from **17.4%** to **7.9%**.

For AI agents handling extended workflows, this is a meaningful improvement.

## Deployment Remains Developer Friendly

Tencent has made deployment relatively straightforward. Hy3 supports:

- **vLLM**
- **SGLang**
- OpenAI-compatible APIs
- FP8 quantized models
- Speculative decoding using MTP

Developers can deploy the model using eight high-memory GPUs, such as NVIDIA H20-class hardware, and immediately access it through the familiar OpenAI Chat Completions API.

The project also includes:

- Finetuning pipeline
- Quantization toolkit (AngelSlim)
- Apache 2.0 license
- FP8 model weights

This lowers the barrier for organizations looking to customize or self-host the model.

## Why Hy3 Matters

Hy3 represents something larger than another benchmark release. It highlights several trends shaping open-source AI in 2026.

- First, **Mixture-of-Experts architectures are becoming the standard** for delivering flagship performance without activating hundreds of billions of parameters.
- Second, **post-training quality is becoming more important than simply increasing parameter count**. Better reinforcement learning, cleaner datasets, and stronger instruction tuning are producing larger gains than raw scaling alone.
- Third, the industry is shifting its focus from chatbot performance to **production-ready AI agents**. Reliability, tool use, long-context reasoning, and multi-turn conversations now matter just as much as benchmark scores.

Finally, Tencent’s decision to release Hy3 under the **Apache 2.0 license** makes it particularly appealing for enterprises that want the flexibility to deploy, fine-tune, and integrate advanced AI models without restrictive licensing.

## Final Thoughts

Hy3 is more than an incremental update over Hy3 Preview.

> It combines a **295B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts architecture**, a **256K context window**, improved reinforcement learning, stronger agent capabilities, and production-focused engineering into a model that competes with many of today’s flagship open-source systems.

While proprietary models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus continue to lead in several specialized benchmarks, Hy3 demonstrates that open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, not just in raw benchmark performance, but in the qualities that matter for real-world deployment.
